rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to observe all 10 compounds while retaining early peaks. The retention spread and critical-pair resolutions will guide subsequent adjustments to gradient range, duration, and temperature.

Halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty while testing how much of the current resolution margin can be traded for speed. Keep temperature and solvent endpoints fixed to isolate the gradient-slope effect.

Test temperature-driven selectivity at the fast gradient, aiming to separate the crowded middle peaks without restoring the long run time. Holding the gradient fixed makes the temperature effect directly assessable.

Slightly lengthen the gradient at 55 C to improve the remaining critical separation. The last peak should still elute near 7.6 minutes, potentially preserving the zero time penalty while achieving full resolution credit.

Test a slightly shallower gradient near the maximum-scoring method to explore resolution margins. The modest slope change should keep the last peak near 8 minutes, although maintaining zero time penalty is not guaranteed.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; test a 5 C increase to explore whether faster elution and stronger critical-pair separation can coexist. Keep the gradient unchanged to isolate temperature-dependent selectivity.

Test the lower-temperature neighbor of the maximum-scoring method to map its selectivity window. This should improve the earlier critical pair but may tighten the later pair, while keeping the last peak near the zero-penalty time limit.

Test initial organic fraction as a new selectivity lever while retaining the successful temperature. A modest increase may shorten retention and shift the balance between the two critical pairs, potentially preserving the maximum CRF.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to raise the remaining critical-pair resolution from 1.29 toward 1.5 while retaining the improved separation of the later pair. The last peak is expected before 8 minutes, making another maximum-scoring method plausible.

Reduce the gradient slope one more step to bring the earlier critical pair above 1.5 while likely preserving the later pair’s resolution. The last peak is predicted near 8 minutes, testing a potentially better-resolved maximum-CRF method at the time-penalty boundary.

Combine a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to offset the retention-time increase while improving middle-peak separation. This tests whether maximum CRF can be maintained with more balanced resolution margins and a last peak before 8 minutes.

This gradient slope lies between injections 9 and 10, targeting both critical-pair resolutions above 1.5 with the last peak around 7.8 minutes. It may match the maximum CRF while providing more balanced resolution and time margins.

The maximum score is already secured, so explore a distinct low-temperature selectivity regime using the fast scouting gradient. Cooling may separate the crowded middle peaks in a different order while keeping the last peak near the zero-time-penalty window.

Test whether higher initial organic content and a faster gradient at 60 C move the earlier critical pair beyond its apparent selectivity crossover into a resolved reversed order. This explores a substantially faster alternative while retaining the established maximum-scoring methods as the benchmark.

Increase the starting organic fraction one step to test whether the apparent reversed critical pair separates further while shortening retention. Monitor the first pair closely, since its resolution may decline as early retention decreases.

Return to the starting composition that resolved the early pair, and steepen the gradient to test separation beyond the apparent middle-pair crossover. This explores a faster maximum-score candidate, though compression may create another limiting pair.

Preserve injection 4’s successful gradient slope and temperature while lowering the final organic fraction. Since its last peak eluted at 7.60 minutes, before this gradient reaches its endpoint, this method should retain the maximum CRF without requiring 95% organic.

Keep the successful gradient slope through the first nine peaks, then hold at 50% organic. This tests whether the last compound can still elute by 8 minutes, preserving maximum CRF with a lower solvent endpoint.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 10 to improve the earlier critical pair while likely retaining adequate later-pair resolution. Injection 18 confirms that zero time penalty extends beyond 8 minutes, so the predicted last peak near 8.2 minutes may still permit maximum CRF.

Preserve injection 10’s starting composition, gradient slope, and temperature while lowering the endpoint to 60% organic. Because all peaks previously eluted before this gradient would end at the outlet, this should retain its maximum CRF and minimum resolution of 1.58.

Lengthen injection 11’s gradient to improve its limiting resolution of 1.10 while retaining the stronger separation of the later critical pair. This tests whether a higher-starting-organic method can reach full resolution before incurring a time penalty.

Reduce the slope slightly from injection 21 to raise its limiting resolution above 1.5 while preserving the later pair’s margin. The last peak is predicted near 9 minutes, testing whether this better-balanced separation can still achieve maximum CRF without a time penalty.

Test a slightly shallower slope than injection 19, targeting stronger separation of the earlier critical pair while keeping the later pair above 1.5. The predicted last peak near 8.4 minutes lies within the demonstrated zero-penalty window, so maximum CRF should remain attainable.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 22 to improve its limiting pair toward R = 1.6 while retaining the later pair’s margin. The last peak should elute just beyond 9 minutes, probing the time-penalty boundary near this maximum-scoring region.

Test a lower-endpoint method with a slightly shallower slope than injection 23, aiming to retain both critical-pair resolutions above 1.5. The last peak is expected near 8.7 minutes, within the demonstrated zero-penalty window, making another maximum-CRF result plausible.
